description_full: Stanley Black & Decker, Inc. provides hand tools, power tools, outdoor products, and related accessories in the United States, Canada, Other Americas, Europe, and Asia. Its Tools & Outdoor segment offers professional grade corded and cordless electric power tools and equipment, including drills, impact wrenches and drivers, grinders, saws, routers, concrete prep and placement tools, and sanders; pneumatic tools and fasteners; corded and cordless electric power tools; household power tools, hand-held vacuums, and small appliances; leveling and layout tools, planes, hammers, demolition tools, clamps, vises, knives, saws, chisels, and industrial and automotive tools; drill, screwdriver, router bits, abrasives, saw blades, and threading products; tool boxes, sawhorses, medical cabinets, and engineered storage solutions; and electric and gas-powered lawn and garden products. This segment sells its products under the DEWALT, CRAFTSMAN, CUB CADET, STANLEY, BLACK+DECKER, and HUSTLER brands through retailers, third-party distributors, independent dealers, and a direct sales force. Its Industrial segment provides threaded fasteners, blind rivets and tools, blind inserts and tools, drawn arc weld studs and systems, engineered plastic and mechanical fasteners, self-piercing riveting systems, precision nut running systems, micro fasteners, high-strength structural fasteners, axel swage, latches, heat shields, pins, couplings, fitting, and other engineered products. This segment sells its products through direct sales force and third-party distributors to the automotive, manufacturing, electronics, construction, aerospace, and other industries. Stanley Black & Decker, Inc. has a strategic partnership with I4F Licensing Nv. The company was formerly known as The Stanley Works and changed its name to Stanley Black & Decker, Inc. in March 2010. The company was founded in 1843 and is headquartered in New Britain, Connecticut.

financial_summary: Stanley Black & Decker, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $16.5B market cap on $15.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -4% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $688M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 7.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 3% operating margin trails the Industrials median (9%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.25x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-36.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 45% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 1.09, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.52 vs 5y 1.12), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $148.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 63% in the 2022 bear market and 54% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $74.08 (margin of safety -50%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 16%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $18.90 to $211 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 281% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $115 on average, 4% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 11.1% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.5%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.68).
It runs a 35% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.42x.
ROE of 4% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 7.1x net debt to EBITDA ($280.1M of cash against $5.9B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.8x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.7% over 3 years, 3.0% over 5 years and 3.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -16.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (1.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 7, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.1% a year to shareholders (0.1% in buybacks and 3.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 3.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 43,500 employees, each generates about $348K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 4.0% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $16K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (7x revenue per employee).
